1. Core Clinical Tension: A 37-year-old previously healthy male pharmacist presents with an acute 8-day history of high spiking fevers and watery diarrhea, preceded by 1 month of constitutional malaise and 6 kg weight loss. Physical examination demonstrates right lower quadrant abdominal tenderness and moderate ascites. Peritoneal fluid analysis reveals a high serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG 1.5 g/dL) simulating portal hypertensive / transudative ascites, and peritoneal AFB smear and PCR are negative. The diagnostic challenge is distinguishing acute bacterial gastroenteritis / intra-abdominal sepsis, decompensated occult portal hypertension, Crohn's disease or appendiceal malignancy, from primary appendicular tuberculosis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs following emergency triage assessment, vital signs, physical examination, initial hematologic/inflammatory markers, baseline hepatic and renal panels, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, and transthoracic echocardiogram, prior to diagnostic paracentesis with fluid analysis, send-out blood/urine cultures, abdominal contrast CT, exploratory laparotomy, and surgical histopathology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute bacterial enterocolitis or gastrointestinal sepsis is considered given high fever, diarrhea, leukocytosis, and right lower quadrant tenderness, but blood and urine cultures remain sterile and the patient fails to respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem, ofloxacin, metronidazole). Cirrhosis or portal hypertension suggested by transudative SAAG is ruled out by normal liver architecture and absence of portal hypertension or cardiac failure. The definitive diagnosis of appendicular tuberculosis is established by surgical histopathology of the resected appendix showing numerous caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells in the serosa and mesoappendix.
case_prompt:
A 37-year-old previously healthy Sri Lankan male pharmacist presents to a tertiary care hospital with an 8-day history of intermittent high spiking fevers. Concurrent with the onset of fever, he developed frequent, small-volume, watery loose stools without visible blood, mucus, or tenesmus. He denies cough, hemoptysis, dysuria, headache, or acute abdominal colic. Over the preceding month, he experienced persistent malaise, progressive anorexia, and an unintentional 6-kg weight loss. He has no history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, or chronic liver disease, and reports no known personal history or household contacts with chronic pulmonary illnesses, though he works as a hospital pharmacist with daily public interactions.

On physical examination, he appears moderately pale, non-icteric, and in mild distress. He is tachycardic with a pulse rate of 120 beats per minute, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, and tachypneic. Precordial examination reveals normal heart sounds without murmurs. Pulmonary examination is normal with clear vesicular breath sounds throughout. Abdominal examination reveals a distended abdomen with mild localized tenderness in the right lower quadrant, with no guarding, rigidity, or hepatosplenomegaly; shifting dullness demonstrates a moderate volume of free peritoneal fluid. There is no peripheral lymphadenopathy or peripheral edema.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL, white blood cell count of 16,000/µL with 70% neutrophils, and platelet count of 560,000/µL. Systemic inflammatory markers are markedly elevated, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 120 mm/1st hour and C-reactive protein of 290 mg/L. Liver biochemistry demonstrates alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 112 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 88 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 230 U/L, with a normal total bilirubin and serum albumin of 3.5 g/dL. Urinalysis is normal. Plain chest radiography is unremarkable. Two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates normal cardiac function without valvular murmurs or pericardial effusion.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute diarrheal onset with high fevers, leukocytosis, and right lower quadrant tenderness initially suggested acute gastrointestinal sepsis or typhlitis, but blood and urine cultures were sterile, and the patient had persistent fever spikes and elevated inflammatory markers despite multi-agent intravenous antibiotics (meropenem, ofloxacin, and metronidazole).
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Three blood cultures and a urine culture did not isolate any pathogen.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG 1.5 g/dL) typically reflects sinusoidal portal hypertension, but the patient had normal serum bilirubin, intact cardiac function without pericardial effusion, and absence of hepatic stigmata.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) was 1.5 g/dL (serum albumin: 3.5 g/dL).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Surgical excision of the appendix and histopathologic examination of the serosa and mesoappendix revealing multiple granulomas composed of epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells with spotty central caseous necrosis established the diagnosis of appendicular tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Microscopically acute inflammation was not present. Serosa and mesoappendix show numerous granulomata composed of epithelioid cells and Langerhans giant cells. Many show central spotty caseous necrosis

editor_comments: Distilled successfully following Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt strictly excludes post-admission paracentesis, laparotomy, histopathology, cultures, and tuberculosis nomenclature.
